## Overview

Western X disease, caused by a phytoplasma that leafhoppers carry from tree
to tree, has spread through the cherry orchards of the Pacific Northwest
since 2015. Infected trees bear small, pale, unmarketable fruit, there is no
cure, and the infection is invisible for a year or more before symptoms
appear. @Ghorbani2026 modelled an acre of cherries as a grid of trees passing
through five disease states, and asked what removing, replanting and testing
trees is worth over 25 years. Their main analysis lets a grower choose
actions from uncertain beliefs about which trees are infected (a partially
observable Markov decision process, solved by rollout); they compare it with
fixed strategies.

This implementation is an **adaptation**. It implements the orchard and the
fixed strategies, not the decision model. The source does not give the
monthly rates of infection or the point at which a block is not harvested;
both are calibrated below to its results without management.

```{julia}
#| output: false
ENV["GKSwstype"] = "100"
using EcologicalCellularAutomata
using CellularAutomataCore
using Plots
using Statistics
```

## The model

The orchard is 20 × 30 trees, planted together. Each month:

- an unvisited tree is inoculated by a leafhopper with probability
  `α + β k` a year (converted to a month), where `k` counts the symptomatic
  trees among its eight neighbours: `α = 1.5%` covers leafhoppers from
  elsewhere, and each symptomatic neighbour adds `β`;
- a visited (inoculated) tree becomes infected, an infected one visible
  (symptomatic), and a visible one high, each with probability 1/2 at every
  full year it has spent in its state;
- trees age, and yield and cost by age, as in the source's crop budget;
  disease cuts the yield by 10, 25, 50 and 75% in the four states.

Between 2 and 8% of the trees start visited.

```{julia}
prob = problem(:western_x_orchard; seed=1)
sol = solve(prob; saveat=12)
colours = cgrad([:white, :forestgreen, :khaki, :orange, :red, :darkred], 6; categorical=true)
plot([heatmap(sol.u[y + 1].state; c=colours, clims=(-0.5, 5.5), aspect_ratio=1,
              colorbar=y == 10, xticks=false, yticks=false, title="year $y",
              titlefontsize=10) for y in (0, 4, 7, 10)]...;
     layout=grid(1, 4; widths=[0.22, 0.22, 0.22, 0.34]), size=(900, 210))
```

States from green (unvisited) through yellow (visited), orange (infected) and
red (visible) to dark red (high). Infection spreads from the first trees to
their neighbours, and the orchard is largely diseased within a decade.

## Calibrating the unknowns

The source gives `β` as 10 to 20% a symptomatic tree, without saying whether
that is a yearly or a monthly probability, and says that growers stop
harvesting a badly diseased block without saying when. Its baseline without
management has a total yield of 103,516 lb an acre over 25 years and a net
present value of -$166,765; yields fall to zero by year 15 (its Fig. 5).
Read as a monthly probability, even the smallest `β` leaves the orchard 40%
symptomatic by year 6. Read as yearly, `β = 0.2` with no harvest once 25% of
the trees are symptomatic gives, over 100 runs:

```{julia}
runs(; n=100, kwargs...) =
    fetch.([Threads.@spawn solve(problem(:western_x_orchard; seed=s, kwargs...); saveat=1)
            for s in 1:n])
function summarise(sols; kw...)
    es = [western_x_economics(s; kw...) for s in sols]
    return (yield=round(Int, mean(sum(e.yield) for e in es)),
            npv=round(Int, mean(e.npv for e in es)),
            yearly=mean(reduce(hcat, [e.yield for e in es]); dims=2)[:])
end
baseline = summarise(runs())
healthy = summarise(runs(; n=1, disease=false))
(baseline=(baseline.yield, baseline.npv), healthy=(healthy.yield, healthy.npv))
```

against the source's 103,516 lb and -$166,765 for the baseline, and 424,959 lb
and $170,046 for an orchard without disease.

```{julia}
plot(1:25, [healthy.yearly baseline.yearly]; marker=:circle, ms=3, lw=1.5,
     label=["no disease" "no management"], xlabel="year", ylabel="yield (lb an acre)",
     size=(650, 340), legend=:topright)
scatter!([4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 15],
         [12000, 17200, 15700, 13400, 10800, 7200, 3700, 1400, 400, 0]; color=:black,
         marker=:x, ms=6, label="source, no management")
```

The crosses are read from the source's Fig. 5. The yield here holds up a
little longer and then falls more steeply, but the totals agree. The value of
the disease to a grower, the difference in net present value, is about
$349,000 an acre here and $337,000 in the source.

The source's damage equation multiplies a diseased tree's cost, as well as
its yield, by its damage factor. Doing so would make diseased trees cheap to
keep, and the baseline's value about -$46,000; costs are not scaled here.

## Removing, replanting and testing

The source's fixed strategies, deciding every other year: cut every
symptomatic tree once 1% of the trees are symptomatic, with or without
replanting (its scenarios 2 and 3); and, from year 4, also test a tenth of
the trees around each symptomatic tree, at $300 a test, cutting those found
infected (its scenarios 6 and 7). The source does not say how many trees it
tests:

```{julia}
strategies = [(:threshold_cut, 270_564, 67_291), (:threshold_replant, 399_438, 105_225),
              (:test_cut, 257_196, 55_867), (:test_replant, 405_732, 116_763)]
results = Dict(s => summarise(runs(; strategy=s)) for (s, _, _) in strategies)
[(strategy=s, yield=results[s].yield, source_yield=y, npv=results[s].npv, source_npv=v)
 for (s, y, v) in strategies]
```

Every strategy is worth more than $220,000 an acre over doing nothing, here
as in the source, and replanting adds yield. The agreement is otherwise rough.
Cut-only is worth more here, and cut and replant yields less. Testing lowers
the value of both here, while the source finds that testing with replanting
gives the most value of its fixed strategies: its testing finds more hidden
infections for its cost than the share and the timing assumed here allow.

## The removal threshold

The source's Fig. 6 asks how long a grower can wait: the net present value of
removal against the share of symptomatic trees at which it starts. Forty runs
each:

```{julia}
thresholds = (0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.15, 0.2, 0.25, 0.3)
sweep = Dict((s, θ) => summarise(runs(; n=40, strategy=s, pmap=(; threshold=θ))).npv
             for s in (:threshold_cut, :threshold_replant) for θ in thresholds)
cut = [sweep[(:threshold_cut, θ)] for θ in thresholds]
replant = [sweep[(:threshold_replant, θ)] for θ in thresholds]
plot(100 .* collect(thresholds), [cut replant] ./ 1000; marker=:circle, lw=2,
     label=["cut" "cut and replant"], xlabel="threshold (% symptomatic)",
     ylabel="net present value (k\$)", size=(650, 360))
scatter!(100 .* collect(thresholds), [67, 25, -45, -100, -113, -110, -113]; color=1,
         marker=:x, ms=6, label="source, cut")
scatter!(100 .* collect(thresholds), [105, 97, 48, 30, 10, -15, -15]; color=2, marker=:x,
         ms=6, label="source, cut and replant")
hline!([0]; color=:gray, ls=:dash, label="")
```

As in the source, waiting costs money, and replanting keeps removal paying
at higher thresholds: cutting and replanting stops paying at about 20%
symptomatic here and 22% in the source. Cut-only loses value more slowly with
the threshold here than in the source, where it stops paying at about 7%.
